passage: When I moved into the hostel, I thought laundry, food and cleaning would take an hour a week. By day nine my bucket was full of clothes, my mug had grown a green skin, and there was no clean shirt. Anand, my roommate, looked at the pile and said only, "So it starts." I felt astonished at how fast everything piles up when nobody does it. That weekend I made a few small rules: wash the mug the moment it is empty, wash two shirts every night, and write the shopping list on the wall when something runs out. Two weeks later, the pile was gone, and I hardly noticed the work. Imran

qa.q: How many days had passed when Imran's bucket was full of clothes?
qa.a: The bucket was full of clothes by day nine.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when looking at the pile of clothes and the mug?
qa.a: Imran felt surprised and a little dismayed at how quickly things pile up when nobody does them.

qa.q: What small habits did Imran adopt to prevent a large weekly mess?
qa.a: Imran began washing the mug as soon as it was empty, washing two shirts every night and writing a shopping list on the wall.

qa.q: How might Anand see Imran's first week in the hostel?
qa.a: Anand, who says "So it starts", seems to have seen it all before and is amused, though not unkind.

grounding: Shows a hostel student surprised by how quickly laundry, dishes and groceries pile up, and using small daily habits.

passage: Hostel warden's note, Monday. Leela moved into the rented room two floors up two weeks ago. On day nine I passed her door and saw a tower of clothes on the bed, a cold pan on the floor and an empty grocery bag. She looked embarrassed. I did not lecture. I asked how the week was going. She shrugged and said, "Nobody told me it would pile up so fast." We sat on the step, and she wrote a plan on the back of a notebook: one plate a day, laundry every Saturday, grocery list on Sunday. This morning the room was tidy and the bed was clear. Gautam, warden

qa.q: How many weeks ago did Leela move into the rented room?
qa.a: Leela moved into the rented room two weeks ago.

qa.q: What was Leela probably feeling when Gautam saw the tower of clothes?
qa.a: Leela was probably embarrassed and surprised by how fast things had piled up, since she shrugged and said nobody had told her.

qa.q: What small step helped Leela keep the room tidy?
qa.a: Leela wrote a plan of one plate a day, laundry every Saturday and a grocery list on Sunday.

qa.q: How does Gautam see Leela's messy room?
qa.a: Gautam sees a student learning something new and treats it gently, asking how the week is going instead of lecturing.

grounding: Shows a student living away from home for the first time surprised at how quickly laundry, dishes and groceries pile up, and using small daily habits.

passage: Uday, you're moving to the hostel next week. Let your Bua, Gurleen, tell you about my first month in Chandigarh when I was eighteen. I'd never washed a single shirt. Beeji did everything at home. By day ten, I had a mountain of clothes under my bed and nothing clean to wear to class. My room smelled of old dal because I'd left a tiffin open. I had instant noodles four nights running. One night, standing in a borrowed kurta, I cried from pure surprise at how fast it had all piled up. My roommate taught me her rule: one bucket of washing every evening, one quick sweep, dishes washed straight after eating. Small things, every day. The mountain never came back.

qa.q: What did Gurleen have under the bed by day ten?
qa.a: A mountain of clothes.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel standing in a borrowed kurta?
qa.a: Gurleen felt overwhelmed and surprised, crying at how fast everything had piled up.

qa.q: Which choice in the story stopped the mess from building again?
qa.a: Following the roommate's rule of one bucket of washing, a quick sweep and washing dishes straight after eating, every day.

qa.q: How might the roommate have seen Gurleen that night?
qa.a: The roommate probably felt sympathetic, seeing a newcomer overwhelmed, and offered a simple daily habit.

grounding: An elder recalls being surprised by how quickly laundry, dishes and mess piled up in the first month away from home.

passage: Chetan, nineteen, moved into a PG in Pune for his engineering course. In week two, the building's water supply started coming only from six to eight in the morning. He hadn't planned for that. By Friday, his bucket of dirty clothes was full, his steel plate had dried dal stuck to it, and he had no clean socks. His neighbour Disha, from the room across, saw him scrubbing a plate at midnight with a bottle of drinking water. "You have to do a little every morning while the water runs," she said. "Otherwise it all waits for you." Chetan groaned. The next morning, at six, he washed two shirts and his plate. It took twelve minutes.

qa.q: When did the water supply come in week two?
qa.a: Only from six to eight in the morning.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel scrubbing a plate at midnight?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and surprised at how quickly everything had piled up.

qa.q: What small habit did Chetan start, and why does it help?
qa.a: Washing a little every morning while the water runs, which prevents a big weekly mess.

qa.q: How does Disha see Chetan's midnight scrubbing?
qa.a: Disha sees it as the result of not doing small tasks daily, and offers practical advice.

grounding: Shows a student living away for the first time surprised by how quickly chores pile up, and learning small daily habits.

passage: Preeti and Yamini, both eighteen, had moved into a rented room near their college in Kolkata. For the first week it felt like freedom: no one telling them to tidy up. By the third week, the sink was full, the dustbin smelled, and they had run out of rice without noticing. On Sunday, they spent four hours cleaning, arguing over who had used the last clean towel. Preeti sat on the floor, exhausted. "At home, it just happened. I never saw it." Yamini nodded. They wrote three rules on the fridge: wash your plate after eating, take out the bin every other day, check the rice jar on Fridays. By the next Sunday, there was nothing to clean.

qa.q: How long did the Sunday cleaning take?
qa.a: They spent four hours cleaning.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling, sitting on the floor?
qa.a: Preeti felt exhausted and surprised, realising how much housework had happened unseen at home.

qa.q: What did the three rules on the fridge change?
qa.a: Small daily habits replaced a big weekly clean, so by the next Sunday there was nothing to clean.

qa.q: How might Yamini see their first weeks of freedom now?
qa.a: Yamini likely sees that the freedom came with hidden work, and agrees that small rules beat a big mess.

grounding: Shows two students living away for the first time surprised by the pile-up of chores and learning daily habits.

passage:
"Kunal, what is that smell?"
"Hi, Rajni didi. Welcome to my room."
"Is that dal? From when?"
"Monday. Maybe Sunday. I was going to wash the pot."
"It's Friday. And why are there clothes on the chair, the bed and the door?"
"Laundry day is Saturday. I was going to do it all then."
"All of it is how much?"
"Basically everything I own." He laughed, then stopped. "Didi, how did it get like this? Two weeks ago it was clean. I didn't do anything."
"That's exactly how. Nothing, every day." She tied her hair up. "Okay. The pot soaks now. You wash your plate the minute you eat. One bucket of clothes every Wednesday, not a mountain on Saturday. And make a list before the shop, or you'll keep buying biscuits and no rice."
"You sound like Ma."
"Ma is right sometimes."

qa.q: Which day did Kunal say the dal was from?
qa.a: Monday, maybe Sunday.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he asked how the room got like this?
qa.a: He was surprised and a bit embarrassed, his laugh stopping as he realised the mess had grown in only two weeks.

qa.q: Which of Rajni's suggestions would stop the pile-up, and why?
qa.a: Washing each plate straight after eating and doing one bucket every Wednesday keeps things small daily, instead of leaving a mountain for Saturday.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel walking into the room?
qa.a: Rajni is probably amused and a little worried, but she treats it kindly and practically, tying her hair up to help rather than scolding.

grounding: Shows a student living away for the first time who is surprised by how fast dishes and laundry pile up, and learns that small daily habits prevent it.
